554.title: The thread of compassion
554.hook: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot and truth the twist (Asa di Var, ang 471)
554.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the janamsakhi story of young Nanak and the sacred thread, and hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var as a call to wear the inner thread of compassion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vaariaa, and your line: the turning point. Did you thank someone? Today, a turning point from Guru Nanak's own childhood, and the salok the tradition ties to it. Day five hundred fifty-four.

The courtyard is full. Relatives have come from nearby villages, food is cooking, and the family priest has arrived for an important day: a boy's investiture with the sacred thread. The boy is Nanak, still young, in Talwandi. The janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak written down generations later, tell what happened next. As the priest prepared the thread, the boy asked him a question. What is this thread for? Will it last? And then he described the thread he would actually wear, and it wasn't made of cotton at all.
screen: `A COURTYARD FULL OF RELATIVES.` → `THE BOY NANAK AND THE THREAD.` → `A THREAD NOT MADE OF COTTON.`

segments.voice: The janeu is a sacred thread that Hindu families in some communities give their sons in a coming-of-age ceremony, worn across the body from the shoulder. For the families who keep it, it marks a second birth into learning and duty, and it's held with real reverence. The salok on ang 471, which Sikh tradition links to young Nanak's day, doesn't mock the thread. It asks for a deeper one. In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul. If you have it, priest, then put it on me. Daiaa, compassion, is the raw cotton, the stuff everything else is spun from. Santokh, contentment, which we met in the servants' pauri, is the thread itself, the long continuous strand. Jat, restraint, self-control, is the knot that holds it together. And sat, truth, is the twist that gives a thread its strength. Untwisted fiber pulls apart in the hands; spinners know it. Truth is what makes the whole thing hold. Notice the order. Compassion comes first, as the material. Everything after that is shaping it. So a person could carry contentment and restraint and even truth, but without compassion there's nothing to spin. Sikhs remember this story as an early sign of who Nanak would become: not someone who rejects people's rituals for the sake of it, but someone always asking what's inside them. Tomorrow, we look at what he said such a thread could survive.
screen: `THE JANEU: A SACRED THREAD.` · `COMPASSION, THE COTTON.` · `CONTENTMENT, RESTRAINT, TRUTH.` · `TRUTH IS THE TWIST THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION IS THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a thread and name the four. If you have a piece of string, yarn, or even a hair tie, hold it. If not, use your fingers. Touch it once and say, in your mind: compassion, the cotton. Run your fingers along it: contentment, the thread. Tie a loose knot: restraint, the knot. Give it a gentle twist: truth, the twist. Then hold it in your palm and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Janeu. The sacred thread. In Guru Nanak's salok, a thread of the soul: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist.
Your line: compassion is the thread. Today, if you tied a string, keep it in your pocket. Each time you touch it, do one small kind thing. Day five hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 554 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THREAD THAT WON'T BREAK.`

555.title: The thread that won't break
555.hook: such a thread doesn't break, burn, get dirty or wear out (Asa di Var, ang 471)
555.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that virtues and the praise of the One are what go with a person beyond death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janeu, and your line: compassion is the thread. Did you keep a string in your pocket? Today, the second half of that same salok, and four things the thread of the soul can survive. Day five hundred fifty-five.

Open any drawer at home and you'll find something that wore out. A sweater with elbows gone thin. A phone cable split near the plug. A favorite shirt washed one too many times. Everything made of fiber frays eventually. Cotton breaks under strain. It burns in a second near a flame. It picks up stains. And even if you protect it from all of that, time thins it out. Guru Nanak knew all four of those ways a thread can fail, and he named them, one by one, about the thread of compassion we tied yesterday.
screen: `A SWEATER WITH THIN ELBOWS.` → `EVERY FIBER FRAYS.` → `FOUR WAYS A THREAD FAILS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the salok on ang 471 continues, in paraphrase. Such a thread doesn't break. It doesn't get dirty. It doesn't burn. It isn't lost. Blessed, Nanak says, are the people who go about wearing it around their necks. Four nots. One way to hear them: breaking is strain: the hard week, the argument, the shock. Dirt is the slow grime of daily life: resentment, envy, gossip. Burning is the sudden fire: rage, disaster, loss. And being lost is time itself, the way things simply slip away. A cotton thread can't survive any of these for long. A thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth, the salok says, survives all four. Then Guru Nanak looks at the outer thread with plain eyes. It's bought for a few coins, he says, and put on in a ceremony. And when the body dies, it falls away; the person leaves without it. Whatever is tied to the body goes the way of the body. The next salok in the var adds a line that answers it. Through trust in the Name, honor arises, and praise of the One is the true thread. Worn that way, it doesn't break in the Court of the Lord. Sikh teaching reads this as a question about what goes with us. Not possessions, not status, not even the symbols we're given. What goes is what we've become. A grandmother who has worn that thread for decades, patient at the stove, honest at the market, takes it with her. The cotton one stays behind.
screen: `IT WON'T BREAK, STAIN, BURN, OR BE LOST.` · `THE OUTER THREAD FALLS AWAY.` · `PRAISE IS THE TRUE THREAD.` · `WHAT GOES IS WHAT WE'VE BECOME.` · then, large: `IT WON'T WEAR OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think what in you won't wear out. Sit and breathe slowly. Picture yourself many years from now, much older, with most of today's worries long gone. Ask: what in me will still be there? Not a job title. Not a look. Maybe a way of listening. A patience you've been building. A love for certain people. Let one quality come forward. Picture it as a thread, already strong, getting stronger. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Compassion, one strand of the soul's thread: in Guru Nanak's salok, spun with contentment, restraint and truth, it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost, and it goes with you.
Your line: it won't wear out. Today, when something breaks or frays, a cable, a plan, your patience, say the line and give a minute to the quality you named. Day five hundred fifty-five.

556.title: The impurity of greed
556.hook: the impurity of the mind is greed, of the tongue lying (Asa di Var, ang 472)
556.howItsDone: Sikh practice keeps no period of ritual impurity after a birth or death; the Sikh Rehat Maryada sets such observances aside, and Sikhs hear these saloks in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion, and your line: it won't wear out. What quality did you name? Yesterday Guru Nanak looked inside a thread. Today he looks inside an old idea of being unclean. Day five hundred fifty-six.

Clean and dirty go deeper than germs. Shoes off at the door. Hands washed before eating. A kitchen counter nobody puts a bag on. Families and cultures draw those lines in different places, and they matter. In Guru Nanak's world, there was a strong idea called sootak: a time of ritual impurity that fell on a household after a birth or a death. For a set period, the family was considered unclean, and others might avoid their food. Guru Nanak took that word and asked where impurity really lives.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `SOOTAK: IMPURITY AFTER BIRTH OR DEATH.` → `WHERE DOES IMPURITY LIVE?`

segments.voice: The saloks are on ang 472, and they come in a short run. The first one starts with a practical puzzle. If you believe in sootak, it says, in paraphrase, then sootak is everywhere. There are tiny creatures in cow dung and in firewood. Not a single grain of food is without life. Water itself gives life to everything. So how can anyone keep sootak out? It's already in the kitchen. Then the salok's answer: Nanak, sootak isn't removed that way. Only spiritual wisdom washes it off. The next salok moves the word somewhere new. In paraphrase again: the sootak of the mind is greed. The sootak of the tongue is lying. Tomorrow we'll hear what it says about the eyes and the ears. For today, stay with those first two. Lobh, greed, is the mind's impurity: the restless wanting that never says enough. Koorh, the same word we met in the salok of the false king, is the tongue's. A household can follow every rule after a birth and still have a greedy mind at the table. A person can scrub their hands and still lie with their mouth. Guru Nanak isn't saying cleanliness doesn't matter; Sikh discipline includes bathing before the dawn prayers, and langar kitchens are kept clean. He's saying the impurity that really keeps people from the One isn't on the skin. A third salok finishes the thought: all sootak is doubt, attachment to something second. Birth and death come by the hukam, the divine order. They're not dirt. Greed and lying are.
screen: `SOOTAK: AN OLD IDEA OF IMPURITY.` · `LIFE IS IN EVERY GRAIN.` · `THE MIND'S IMPURITY: GREED.` · `THE TONGUE'S IMPURITY: LYING.` · then, large: `CLEAN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your tongue clean today. Sit and breathe. Rest your attention on your mouth for a moment: the tongue, the lips, the breath passing through. Then think ahead over today's conversations. Notice where a small untruth might slip out: an excuse, an exaggeration, a way of shading a story. Decide now, kindly, that today you'll let your words be plain and true. Let the tongue rest, quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that clean tongue. The bell holds the time.
Sootak. Ritual impurity, once thought to fall on a home after a birth or death. Guru Nanak moves it inside: the mind's sootak is greed, the tongue's is lying.
Your line: clean tongue. Today, catch one small exaggeration before it leaves your mouth, and say the plain version instead. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: Eyes and ears
557.hook: the impurity of the eyes is coveting, of the ears is gossip (Asa di Var, ang 472)
557.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of the four impurities in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching counts avoiding slander and coveting as part of daily discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sootak, and your line: clean tongue. Did you catch an exaggeration and say the plain version? Yesterday's salok named the mind and the tongue. Today it goes on to the eyes and the ears. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Scroll for ten minutes and count what comes in. Someone's new kitchen. Someone's vacation. A car you can't afford. A rumor about a person you've never met, and three hundred comments about it. None of it touched your hands. You didn't say a word. And yet the phone goes down with something new in it: a small want for what's theirs, a small taste for the rumor. Long before any feed, Guru Nanak named the two doors those come in through.
screen: `TEN MINUTES OF SCROLLING.` → `A SMALL WANT, A SMALL TASTE FOR RUMOR.` → `TWO DOORS IT CAME IN THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of the salok on ang 472, in paraphrase. The sootak of the eyes is looking with desire at another's spouse, another's wealth, another's beauty. The sootak of the ears is taking in slander, feeding on gossip. And then the last line: Nanak, even those who seem like swans, pure and bright, are bound and led away, if they carry these. Look at how exact this is. The eyes aren't impure for seeing. They're impure for a certain kind of looking: the look that wants what belongs to someone else. Coveting. It's quiet. Nobody else can see it. But it changes the one doing it, because every look that wants another's life makes your own life look smaller. The ears aren't impure for hearing, either. Gurbani is meant to be heard, sung aloud as kirtan. The impurity is in what the ears are fed. The salok's word for it is laaitbaaree: talebearing, backbiting, the tale carried about someone who isn't there. The salok pictures the ears almost eating it. And gossip, like coveting, doesn't need you to do anything. You just have to listen, and enjoy it a little. Put yesterday and today together and you have four doors: mind, tongue, eyes, ears. Greed, lies, coveting, gossip. Guru Nanak's point across all of it is the same. Washing the outside is easy. Keeping these four doors clean is the real purity, and it happens many times a day, in moments nobody else will ever see.
screen: `THE EYES: COVETING.` · `THE EARS: FEEDING ON GOSSIP.` · `IT CHANGES THE ONE WHO DOES IT.` · `FOUR DOORS: MIND, TONGUE, EYES, EARS.` · then, large: `CLEAN EYES, CLEAN EARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look and listen cleanly. Sit and let your eyes rest on something simple in front of you: a wall, a cup, the sky. Just see it, without wanting it or judging it. Then close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you: traffic, a fan, a bird. Just hear them, without a story. Notice how quiet the mind gets when the eyes and ears simply receive. If you pray, you can let the word Waheguru be the one thing you listen to inside. The bell holds the time.
Laaitbaaree, talebearing or backbiting: in Guru Nanak's salok, the eyes' impurity is coveting what is another's; the ears' impurity, laaitbaaree, is feeding on gossip.
Your line: clean eyes, clean ears. Today, when a conversation turns to someone who isn't there, change the subject, or simply stop listening. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: Speak sweetly
558.hook: speak insipid words and body and mind grow insipid (Asa di Var, ang 473)
558.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok on fikka speech in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and sweet, humble speech is counted among the marks of a Sikh's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday, laaitbaaree, and your line: clean eyes, clean ears. Did you step away from a rumor? Today the var comes back to the tongue, but from the kitchen this time. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Taste a spoonful of dal before the salt goes in. It isn't bad, exactly. It isn't poisoned or burned. It's just flat. Lifeless. You take one bite and push the bowl away. Punjabi has a word for that taste: fikka. Tea without sugar is fikka. A party where nobody talks is fikka. And Guru Nanak used the same kitchen word, in a salok of the Asa di Var, for a certain kind of speech. Not lying, which we met two days ago. Something more ordinary, and maybe more common.
screen: `DAL BEFORE THE SALT.` → `FIKKA: FLAT, TASTELESS.` → `A KITCHEN WORD FOR SPEECH.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 473. In paraphrase: speaking fikka words, the body and mind become fikka. The fikka person is called fikka; the fikka person gets a fikka name. The fikka are cast out of the Court of the Lord, and have their faces spat upon. The fikka are called fools, and are punished with shoes. The word repeats until you can taste it. Fikka here means insipid, but it also leans toward harsh, rude, sour: words with no sweetness and no care in them. A curt reply. A sarcastic dig. A cold one-word answer to someone who needed more. Here's the turn. The salok doesn't only say fikka words hurt the listener. It says they make the speaker fikka. Body and mind. Speak flat and sour long enough, and you become flat and sour. Your reputation follows: people start to call you that. Anyone who's watched a person harden over the years has seen this happen. Words aren't just output. They're practice. Every sentence trains the one who says it. This connects back to mitthat neevee from day five hundred fifty-one: sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue. That was about who you are. Today is about how you get there. Sweet speech isn't flattery or fake niceness. It means words with some care cooked into them. Salt in the dal. Sugar in the tea. Something that makes the other person want to stay at the table.
screen: `FIKKA: FLAT, HARSH, SOUR.` · `FIKKA WORDS MAKE A FIKKA PERSON.` · `EVERY SENTENCE IS PRACTICE.` · `CARE COOKED INTO WORDS.` · then, large: `SWEET WORDS, SWEET LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say something warm. Sit and breathe. Think of the last flat or sharp thing you said to someone, maybe today, maybe yesterday. Don't scold yourself. Just hear it again. Now imagine saying it with care cooked in: the same truth, a warmer sentence. Then think of someone who'd be glad to hear something kind from you. Find the words now: simple, true, warm. Hold them ready. If you pray, you can say Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Speak sweetly. Guru Nanak's warning about fikka words, flat and harsh like dal without salt: they make the body and mind of the speaker fikka too.
Your line: sweet words, sweet life. Today, say your warm words out loud to that person, by phone, in a message, or face to face. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: The servant who argues
559.hook: a servant who serves while arguing proudly loses the master's favor (Asa di Var M2, ang 474)
559.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on the arguing servant in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh seva is meant to be done humbly, without complaint or display.

segments.voice: Yesterday, speak sweetly, and your line: sweet words, sweet life. Who heard your warm words? Today Guru Angad pictures someone who does the work, but can't stop talking back. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

You ask someone at home to take out the trash. They do it. Eventually. But first there's a sigh, then a speech about how they always do everything, then a list of what you haven't done, then the bag dragged slowly to the door. The trash gets taken out. Technically, the job is done. And somehow nobody in the house feels better. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short salok about exactly this kind of service, the kind that gets done with an argument attached.
screen: `THE TRASH, EVENTUALLY.` → `A SIGH, A SPEECH, A LIST.` → `THE JOB DONE, NOBODY BETTER.`

segments.voice: The salok is marked mahala 2, Guru Angad's, on ang 474. In paraphrase: a servant who works for a master, but serves with pride and argues, who talks a great deal, doesn't win the master's pleasure. Then the other picture. One who loses the self and serves gains some honor. And the last line: Nanak, the one who clings to the Master meets the Master; that clinging is accepted. Notice what the arguing servant does right. He shows up. He does the work. The salok doesn't say he's lazy. The problem is everything he wraps around the work: gaarab, pride, and vaad, argument. Endless talk about how hard it is, how unfair, how much better he'd do it if he were in charge. The work gets done, but the service doesn't arrive, because service isn't only an action. It's a way of offering it. Remember the contented servants on day five hundred forty-five. That pauri was Guru Nanak's. This salok is his successor's, and it shows the shadow side of the same picture. The contented served, and were accepted. The proud served too, and argued, and lost the favor. There's a story Sikhs tell about Guru Angad himself, when he was still called Bhai Lehna. Guru Nanak asked for hard and dirty jobs to be done, and while others objected, Lehna simply did them. Tradition holds that's part of why Guru Nanak chose him. Whatever the details, the salok reads like it came from someone who had lived it: serving without the speech.
screen: `PRIDE AND ARGUMENT AROUND THE WORK.` · `THE JOB DONE, THE SERVICE NOT.` · `LOSE THE SELF, GAIN HONOR.` · `BHAI LEHNA SIMPLY DID IT.` · then, large: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without grumbling. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of one task waiting for you today that you'd normally do with a sigh: a chore, a request from someone, an errand. Picture yourself doing it all the way through without the commentary. No sigh. No list. No speech in your head. Just the work, offered. Notice whether something in you resists. Let it, and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture finishing. The bell holds the time.
Gaarab, pride: in Guru Angad's salok, one who serves with gaarab and argument doesn't please the Master; one who loses the self in service gains honor.
Your line: serve without argument. Today, do the task you pictured, and leave out the sigh and the speech entirely. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: How each pauri sums up
560.hook: each pauri gathers the saloks before it into a stanza of its own
560.howItsDone: When Asa di Var is sung at dawn, ragis sing the saloks and then each pauri, and many Sikhs read the var from a gutka, pauri by pauri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gaarab, and your line: serve without argument. Did you leave out the sigh? It's a week's end: the thread of compassion, compassion, sootak, laaitbaaree, sweet speech, gaarab. Today, how the var holds all of them together. Day five hundred sixty.
screen: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.` · `A WEEK: THREADS, PURITY, SPEECH, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Climb a staircase in an old Punjabi house, or the steps down to the water at a gurdwara sarovar, and every step has a name: pauri. The same word is used for a ladder rung. And it's also the name for the stanzas you've been hearing for weeks without quite noticing them. Japji is built of pauris. So is every var in the Guru Granth Sahib. For three weeks we've mostly been listening to saloks, the short verses that tell of trees and threads and scales. Today we look at the steps they're sitting on.
screen: `A STEP DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `PAURI: A STEP, A RUNG.` → `THE STEPS UNDER THE SALOKS.`

segments.voice: A var, as we heard on day five hundred thirty-six, is an old Punjabi ballad form, sung about heroes and battles. Its stanzas are pauris, and in a var they march: each one a step forward in the story. The Guru Granth Sahib has twenty-two vars. In the Asa di Var, the pauris are Guru Nanak's, twenty-four of them, and they carry the main line of the poem: who the One is, how creation stands, what a true servant is like, what the Guru does. Then, in front of each pauri, sit two or more saloks. Some are Guru Nanak's, some Guru Angad's. Many scholars hold that the saloks were set beside the pauris when Guru Arjan compiled the Granth, gathered by theme so they'd open up the step that follows. So the shape works like this. The saloks wander. They look at a silk-cotton tree, a cartload of books, a thread, a kitchen. They make you see something. And then the pauri arrives, and gathers what you've just seen into one step forward. You've felt this already. Remember the pauri where Guru Nanak says he's a sacrifice to the True Guru, who put wisdom on his eyes. It came after saloks about show without substance. The saloks showed the problem, and the pauri named the turning. Here's why it matters for listening. When you hear the Asa di Var sung, you can feel the rhythm: wander, gather; wander, gather. Many small pictures, then one step up. It's a way of learning that doesn't rush. You don't climb the whole staircase at once. You take the next pauri.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD OF HEROES.` · `24 PAURIS, GURU NANAK'S.` · `SALOKS WANDER, THE PAURI GATHERS.` · `WANDER, GATHER; ONE STEP UP.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one pauri whole. If you have a gutka or an app with the Asa di Var, find any pauri and read it slowly, all the way through, in Gurmukhi or in translation. If you don't, hold in your mind the pauri from this week: the contented ones served, did good, ate little, broke the world's chains, and the One kept giving more. Let it sit as one step, complete. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
Pauri. A step, a ladder rung, and a stanza. In the Asa di Var, each of Guru Nanak's twenty-four pauris gathers the saloks before it into one step forward.
Your line: step by step. Today, when a big task feels like a whole staircase, name only the next step, and take it. Day five hundred sixty.
